prime.problem: A network does arithmetic on numbers, but a character is a symbol. Feeding its index (5 for e) invents a fake ordering, and a one-hot vector wastes almost all of its work multiplying by zero.
prime.fits: The previous card turned names into a (32, 3) tensor X of character indices. This card turns each index into a learned vector, the first layer of Bengio's MLP. It builds on the bigram card's one-hot input times a weight matrix.
prime.goal: Explain why reading a row of C is the same computation as a one-hot matmul, predict the shape of C[X] for any index tensor, and build the lookup for the whole dataset in one line.

attend: In one_hot(5) @ C, which of the 27 rows of C actually contribute to the answer, and why does that make indexing a legal shortcut?
Where does the extra axis in C[X] come from, and what would its size be if each character had 10 numbers instead of 2?
What changes about the work and memory of the one-hot route as the vocabulary grows from 27 characters to 17,000 words?
If the forward pass is only a copy, how can C still receive gradients and learn?
Why must the same row be used for a character in every position of the context?

must: one-hot vector has a single 1 → one_hot(i) @ C scales every row by 0 except row i → the product equals C[i] → an embedding is a bias-free linear layer, and indexing is the same math without the wasted multiplies
indexing with a tensor replaces each integer by its row → C[X] has shape X.shape + (row width,) → (32, 3) becomes (32, 3, 2) → the next layer must flatten 3 × 2 = 6 numbers per example

one shared table used at every position and in every context → what the network learns about a character's row carries to all contexts → similar characters can drift together and the model generalises (Bengio's idea)
lookup is mathematically a matmul → gradients reach C like any weight matrix, but only the rows that were looked up → a row used several times sums its gradients; unused rows get exactly zero
elevated: the one-hot route costs vocabulary × width per lookup (27 × 2 = 54 here, 17,000 × 30 = 510,000 for Bengio's words) → a lookup costs only width → this is why real models never build the one-hot tensor
reference: F.one_hot(torch.tensor(5), num_classes=27) needs a tensor, not a Python int
C[[5, 6, 7]] accepts a list; nn.Embedding(27, 2) wraps the same table as a module
the seed 2147483647 used by the lab

compress.prompt: From memory, explain in 3–5 sentences why C[X] is an embedding layer and not a trick. Or draw the path from one integer in X to its vector in emb, and next to it the one-hot matmul that gives the same answer.
checklist: C is a learned table: one row per character
one_hot(i) @ C picks out row i because every other row is multiplied by 0
so indexing computes a linear layer's output without the zero multiplies
C[X] keeps X's shape and appends the row width: (32, 3) → (32, 3, 2)
the same row is shared across positions and contexts, which is what lets learning transfer
gradients still flow into the used rows, so C trains like a weight matrix

retrieve.q: Explain to someone who knows matrix multiplication why C[5] and F.one_hot(torch.tensor(5), 27).float() @ C must print the same numbers.
answer: the one-hot row is 0 everywhere except a 1 at position 5
the product is a weighted sum of C's rows with those weights
every term vanishes except 1 · C[5]

retrieve.q: Walk through emb = C[X] for row 1 of X, the context ..e. What indices are read, and what ends up in emb[1]?
answer: PyTorch reads C[0], C[0], C[5]
emb[1] is a (3, 2) block: two copies of the . row, then e's row

retrieve.q: Your vocabulary grows from 27 characters to 17,000 words with 30-number embeddings. Compare the one-hot matmul with a lookup in work per token and memory. Is there anything the matmul can do that the lookup can't?
answer: matmul: 17,000 × 30 = 510,000 multiply-adds per token and a 17,000-wide mostly-zero input
lookup: copy 30 numbers, no extra tensor
the matmul also accepts a soft blend over tokens; the lookup needs a whole-number id

retrieve.q: You build emb = C[X] and then write W1 = torch.randn((6, 100)). Explain where the 6 comes from and what would break if C had 10 columns.
answer: each example has 3 characters × 2 numbers = 6 inputs after flattening
with 10 columns emb is (32, 3, 10), so 30 inputs
a hard-coded 6 no longer matches and the matmul fails

compare.q: The bigram net multiplied a one-hot by a (27, 27) weight matrix; here we index a (27, 2) table. What is fundamentally the same, what changed in the design, and what does each output mean?
answer: same: both are 'pick a row of a learned matrix' for one character
bigram: the row is 27 logits for the next character directly
here: the row is a small feature vector that later layers combine across 3 characters
the bigram can only use 1 character of context; the embedding lets context grow without a table per context

compare.q: Both a count table and an embedding table are 'one row per something'. Why does the count table explode with context length and the embedding table not?
answer: count table: one row per whole context, 27ⁿ rows (19,683 for n = 3)
embedding table: one row per character, 27 rows no matter the context length
context is handled by concatenating rows and a hidden layer, not by more table rows

compare.q: GPT uses the same lookup for tokens, plus a second table indexed by position. What problem does the position table solve that C[X] in this MLP never had to?
answer: the MLP keeps position by where each embedding sits when flattened (slot 0, 1, 2)
attention mixes tokens without a fixed slot order, so position must be added as its own learned vector
both tables are plain lookups trained by backprop

predict.q: The lecture later switches to C = torch.randn((27, 10)). Before running it: what shape is C[X] for the (32, 3) X, and what must the first dimension of W1 become?
predict.answer: C[X] is (32, 3, 10): the appended axis is the row width. Flattening gives 3 × 10 = 30 numbers per example, so W1 must be (30, …); the lecture's final model uses (30, 200). Any code that hard-coded 6 now breaks, which is why Karpathy prefers view(-1, …) or emb.shape[0] on the next card.

apply.task: Prove the equivalence for the whole batch, not just one index. Using the lab's seeded C and the 5-word X, build F.one_hot(X, num_classes=27).float() @ C and compare it with C[X]. Then, by hand from the table on the card, write out emb[3] (context emm) before printing it.
apply.done: F.one_hot(X, 27).shape is (32, 3, 27), torch.equal(C[X], F.one_hot(X, 27).float() @ C) prints True, and your hand-written emb[3] is (−0.4713, 0.7868), (2.4448, −0.6701), (2.4448, −0.6701).
apply.hint: @ with a 3-D left side treats the first two axes as a batch: (32, 3, 27) @ (27, 2) → (32, 3, 2). X[3] is [5, 13, 13].
